paras: The lynching of Squire Loftin took place near Lexington, Lee County, Texas, in late July 1895, when a mob took Loftin, described as a Black man, from custody and hanged him from a tree. He had been accused of attempting to assault a 12-year-old girl, and the papers reported that he had also confessed to a murder committed seven years earlier. The Shiner Gazette in Texas reported it in some detail, while papers across the Midwest carried it as a brief wire or digest item.

According to a Lexington dispatch in the Shiner Gazette, Loftin was accused of attempting to rape Anna Minehardt, the 12-year-old daughter of a farmer living six miles west of town, as she walked to school on a Tuesday. The same account said he would have carried out the attack had he not been frightened off by some children he took for men. The wire version gave the charge more briefly as assaulting "a white woman."

Loftin was caught two miles below Lincoln and carried to the jail at Giddings. The Shiner Gazette reported that he then confessed to strangling and assaulting a Mrs. Krotchkike at Dimebox seven years before, a killing it said had remained unsolved; a Mississippi brief called the earlier victim a "Bohemian" woman.

In the Shiner Gazette's account, a mob went from Lexington to Giddings and took Loftin out of the jail at 3 a.m., surprising the jailer. Sheriff Scarborough set out with bloodhounds to find the party, but the men eluded him. Loftin was hanged at 5:30 that evening from a tree one mile northwest of Lexington.

A brief in the Port Gibson Reveille gave his name as Squire Loftin and said a large crowd had gathered in the Lexington public square. In that version Sheriff Scarlett went after the mob to rescue the prisoner but arrived too late, and the body was found hanging from a tree. A wire dispatch dated Lexington, July 27, said only that Loftin had been arrested the day before and was "taken from the officers last night and lynched."
No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the mob or an official inquiry appears in the coverage.

The fullest coverage came from the Shiner Gazette, which on August 1 ran the Lexington dispatch under the headline "Negro Lynched" and a shorter version in its "State Condensations" column. It opened with "Once more Judge Lynch has rendered the verdict of death" and presented the reported confession as settling both crimes, "for which he paid his life." Yet the same paper closed by saying the mob had "finished Loftin's career without law."

Outside Texas, the Port Gibson Reveille in Mississippi carried the story among its Texas briefs as "Loftin Lynched at Lexington." The wire dispatch ran under "Negro Lynched" in Dakota papers between August 1 and 2. Weekly news digests in Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Dakota, Ohio, Missouri and Michigan reduced it to a single sentence, "A mob lynched S. Loftin, a negro, charged with assaulting a white woman," set among other lynchings of the week. Those digest versions carried on into August 3 in papers such as the Perrysburg Journal and the Cape Girardeau Democrat.
No coverage of the lynching was found in the Black press.

The accounts differ on the date: the July 25 Lexington dispatch places the hanging on the previous evening, about July 24, while the July 27 wire places the seizure on the night of about July 26. They also differ on where Loftin was seized, at the Giddings jail or from officers after a crowd gathered in Lexington, and on the sheriff's name, given as Scarborough and as Scarlett. The Shiner Gazette's account is local and the most detailed, but no later report settles these points.

Loftin was hanged by a 'mob' that took him from the Giddings jail or from officers, which the Shiner Gazette said 'finished Loftin's career without law' (A2, A5); the mob acted on an accusation of attempted rape and a reported confession to murder (A2, A4).

A Texas local dispatch (A1-A2), a separate Texas news-service brief (A4) and a wire dispatch (A5) independently report the seizure and lynching of Loftin at Lexington, though they differ on date, sheriff's name and place of seizure.
